en: Preface to the *Miscellaneous Records of the Mountain Hermitage*:
The Way is manifested through words, and words are transmitted by virtue. Thus, words born of virtue do not merely command credence for a single generation;
rather, they are transmitted to future ages without doubt. Chan Master Shuzhong retired from his duties at Ruiyan.
He dwelt in seclusion at the Taibai Mountain Hermitage, finding delight in the Way. His single room was desolate and bare, and he stored no surplus possessions.

Students came daily to fill the space outside his door, yet he would not turn them away. Should they receive the benefit of even a single word from him, it was valued more than ten thousand pieces of gold;
it was as if they had drunk sweet nectar or clarified butter, their minds and eyes becoming fully nourished. This was because, throughout his past travels...
Within the gate of the Great Master, whatever was heard or seen—excellent words and virtuous deeds—were internalized with the mind and harmonized with principle.
These were then expressed in speech without the addition of ornamental embellishment; they naturally formed complete compositions.

Whether from the venerable elders of the monastic forests or the eminent scholars of the Confucian school, down to the commoners of the villages and lanes, their words were sufficient to encourage through goodness and sufficient to warn against evil, so that when people heard them...
His mind opened and his understanding was resolved. He committed these thoughts to writing and titled the work *Miscellaneous Records of a Mountain Hermitage*.

His disciple, Hyon Jeokjeong, who resides at Chwiram, carved the woodblocks for its circulation and traveled far to the capital specifically to present it to me. As I read it, I could not put it down;
through this, I came to know that what are called the "words of worldly governance" are all in accord with the True Dharma, whether they be coarse words or gentle speech.
All are the primary meaning; faith does not deceive. It is like all grasses and trees: when a skilled physician gathers them, there is none that is not medicine.
Those who do not understand, however, take the medicine and instead contract an illness. Whether mundane or supramundane, all phenomena are nothing other than the Buddha-dharma.

Those who understand the underlying principles have grasped them; all are sufficient to perpetuate the world and establish the teachings. Is this not what is meant by a Chan Master possessing both virtue and eloquence?
He may be called one who well understands the nature of medicines and illnesses, and one who skillfully discourses upon the Buddha-dharma.
I share the affection of a family connection with this Chan Master; though we have never met face-to-face, we have been acquainted through our reputations for many years.
It is so. For it is well known that his virtue was sufficient to subdue the masses and his words were sufficient to instruct the age;

thus, even had he remained silent, people would have naturally believed him without doubt. How much more so when these are all matters already established, which truly illustrate principles through events and point toward the profound through the proximate.
It is fitting that this shall benefit the present age and be transmitted without end.
Written in the sixth month of the summer in the Jisi year of the Hongwu era, by Hongdao, Left Supervisor of the Office for the Registration of Monks,
preface to the *Miscellaneous Records of Mountain Hermitages*.

Throughout my life I have been frequently ill. In my later years, when I was summoned to the capital following the petition from Japan, I privately thought to myself: "Even if I do not go to Japan, how could I possibly return alive?
Among all my former friends and acquaintances, there was likewise none who did not anticipate this outcome. Fortunately...

The present Emperor took pity on him and specifically stayed the submission of his petition, allowing him to remain at Tien-chiai. Subsequently, various illnesses assailed him simultaneously, and he nearly died three times.

Again, fortunately, the Emperor took pity and granted him permission to return to his former mountain retreat at T'ien-tung. His relatives and old friends came to offer their greetings and inquiries as if he had returned from another life. I, for my part, [regarding] his age...

I am nearly seventy years old; having escaped death ten thousand times to find life once more, I have retired behind closed doors to decline all worldly entanglements so as to exhaust my remaining years.
Among my Dharma-nephews, there is one named Zhuangjing Zhong, who has frequently visited my mountain hermitage and requested of me:

"The great beings of the Tang and Song dynasties who established their teachings and composed writings did so with constant and uninterrupted effort. Since the Yuan dynasty, however, such works have become exceedingly rare."
Therefore, the renowned virtues and sagacious teachings of those from recent antiquity who could serve as models for the monastic community have, for the most part, vanished without a trace.
Yet, during the period when the monastic community was at its zenith, the Master traveled extensively to study under various great elders.
Your learning and insights are vast and profound. Whenever I attend your discourse, I occasionally hear you utter one or two points that I have never heard before, which inspire me most deeply.
I pray that you might, as a matter of playful mastery (*līlā-samādhi*), compose a work of your own;

to illuminate above the hidden brilliance of the former masters and to liberate below the chronic ailments of later students—this would be a great event for the Dharma-gate. I venture to request this of you.
I requested him, saying: "Your aspiration is indeed noble; however, what I have to say is not refined in its expression.
How can that which is not refined suffice to travel far? This is something I dare not presume to undertake. Jingzhong spoke again, saying:
"Now the teachings of the Buddha are in decline, and the predecessors have for the most part perished. That you, Master, would now return from afar is beyond all expectation. You must not decline."
I am unable to bear this burden. To whom, then, shall I entrust it? Whether the language used is elegant or not is of no consequence;
if one can simply record the facts straightforwardly to illuminate the events, that will suffice. I pray you do not firmly decline.

Thus, I have compiled what has been taught by my teachers and friends throughout my life, as well as what I have seen and heard across the lakes and seas—whether it be the striking of karmic conditions or the retribution for good and evil.

It is appropriate that one’s words and deeds, whether in public or in private, regardless of the sequence of time or the status of the person involved—noble or humble—should be recorded as they truly occurred, with honest intent and brush, whenever they may serve to admonish or encourage future generations.
This work is titled *The Miscellaneous Records of the Mountain Hermitage*. It is modeled after the *Luo Hu Ye Lu* (Wild Records of Luo Lake) by the renowned elder of the Song dynasty.
In the *Yunwo Jitan* (Records of Cloud-Dwelling), that which is recorded therein mostly emphasizes the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding such matters as these, what I recorded during my youth and vigor has now already been forgotten seven-eighths.

In my later years, living in seclusion at the edge of the sea, I have been unable to seek out information from other sources or gather it extensively; thus, much has been lost. I regret this greatly. This is because... [the text says].
As for the Way, it may be considered the ultimate teaching, yet I have never spoken of it. To speak beyond this would exceed my proper sphere.
Nevertheless, those who uphold the traditions of Sima Qian and Fan Ye as writers of our school may perhaps find herein something worth adopting.
Preface by the monk Wuchen of Tiantai on the full moon of the twelfth month in the eighth year of Hongwu.
Master Shuzhong, as the eighth-generation descendant of Huqiu, sat upon a great Dharma seat, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. For...

He is the one upon whom both the clergy and the laity rely for refuge. While Master Wuxiang (Jushi Song Gong Lian) has already composed a preface for the *Record of the Second Assembly*, the *Miscellaneous Records of the Mountain Hermitage* remains without a preface.

Therefore, the Chan master’s senior disciples, Xuanji Ding, who currently resides at Mount Shuanglin, and Taoyong Xuan, who formerly resided at Nanming, have joined together in requesting me, Bo-heng, to compose one.
Having read it once or twice, Guo Wei Xuanji addressed Taozhong, saying: "In the past, I had the opportunity to see the records of two assemblies. I immediately praised them, saying:
'How is it that they flow forth so abundantly and overflow, like a thousand rivers originating from a single source?

How is it that they are so thunderous, inviting, swift, and sharp, like lightning striking and a sweeping wind? How is it that they are so harmoniously fused and perfectly complete, showing no trace of chisel or hammerwork? "
How extraordinary! To sever the trailing vines and remove the boundaries, one does not fall into the realm of emotional consciousness.
This indeed flows forth from the True Vehicle; compared to those who pick up bits here and there to apply in practice, the distance between them is no less than ninety thousand li.
By examining his words, one can discern his profound realization; he is truly one who has attained the stages of a Buddha or Bodhisattva. Nevertheless, as he proceeded—
In the past, my efforts were directed toward chanting the *dhāraṇīs* to rouse diligence and proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma; my sole task was to bring my own affairs to completion.

Therefore, I had no leisure for extensive discourse. Now, observing this record, I see that whether in the imperial court, among the prefectures and counties, within the marketplace, or beneath the mountain forests—regarding the people, their conduct, their deeds, and their writings—whether they be good or [otherwise], [they all appear here].
Whether good or not good, whether this or not this, whether timely or not timely, whether superior or not superior—there is nothing it does not encompass.

It can serve as encouragement and it can serve as a warning. Thus, regarding Confucians, Buddhists, Daoists, officials, recluses, the elderly, the refined, the wealthy and noble, the poor and lowly, merchants and peddlers, artisans, and butchers and vintners—[it applies to all].
From farmers and gardeners, down to women and children, and even to servants and slaves, there is none who does not derive benefit from it.
When the clouds of compassion gather and thicken, not a single inch of ground remains uncovered; when the rain of the Dharma falls in torrents, not a blade of grass fails to be moistened.
As the sun and moon rise in the east and set in the west, there is no dark path that they do not illuminate. Through the night...
The soil covers what is above and bears what is below; there is no living being that is not sustained by it. The composition of this record was intended with a mind such as this:

out of great compassion for all sentient beings, employing many skillful means to provide a subtle guidance, so that they may cast off the false and delusory while remaining undeluded regarding true wisdom—equal and without distinction. Such is the Master’s benevolence.
This lies within oneself. One is truly a person of the stage of a Buddha or Bodhisattva if, in the mere instant of a single glance at this, one attains a sudden, transcendent awakening;

beginning from a state where there is neither encouragement nor reprimand, one reaches a state where there is nothing that is not encouraged or reprimanded, and from that state where there is nothing that is not encouraged or reprimanded, one arrives at a state of no encouragement or reprimand.
Thus entering the ground of enlightenment via the correct path, one cannot be driven by habitual tendencies or karmic consciousness.
"It cannot be bound. This is precisely the intent behind Master Chan’s compilation.
Xuji, Taocong, and Jiji have diligently carved blocks for printing and disseminated it; their hearts were likewise the heart of the Master. Alas!

How could this be viewed as a mere ordinary scribble, intended only to broaden one's见闻 (jìnwén—knowledge and views) or to provide material for idle discourse? Having made these remarks, he then wrote [this preface].
Preface. On the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month in the winter of the twenty-fifth year of Hongwu, written by the Layman of No-Name, Su Bocheng of Meishan. Preface.
*Shan'an Zalù*, Volume One, composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Shi Wucun. Master Dingshui Baoye was a native of Siming.
He studied under Xutang of Mount Jing; regarding all the *huatou* of the Chan school that had not yet been... [text continues]
Those who are able to penetrate through must consult and question those of mature experience until they have penetrated through and do not stop. One day, he went to Xutang and asked:
"Regarding Deshan’s final word: if one says it exists, how could Deshan have failed to realize it? If one says it does not exist,"
Yantou said again, "I have not yet understood Master Daoshan. I pray that the Venerable One will compassionately instruct me. Xutang replied, "I do not understand either.
Go and ask Chief Seat Yun. The Master went to ask Chief Seat Yun, who had just returned from a mountain excursion.
He asked for water to wash his feet. The Head Seat hurriedly brought the water forward; the Master leaned his body forward and reached out his hands for him to rub them.
Then, looking up, he asked, "I do not yet know whether Deshan’s final word exists or not; I hope the Head Seat will grant me an instruction.
The Head Seat Yun took both hands, scooped up the water used for washing the feet, and splashed it on him, saying, "What 'final word' is there? The Master did not understand this.
The next day, they went to see Master Xu Tang. Tang asked, "I instructed you to ask Cloud (Yun) the Head Seat about his 'final word.
What did he say? The Master replied, "I followed the Master's command and asked him, but he doused me with the water used for washing his feet."
Huangbo said, "He has no other words. The Master asked, "What did he say? What was that final phrase?
Huangbo said, "I will tell you; he understood it. Thereupon, the Master was relieved. As for the Head Seat Yun, he was Master Xianji.
He was the foremost disciple of Venerable Xutang and possessed noble conduct. He resided at Huqiu and passed away there.
The abbot of Dinghui Temple in Pingjiang, named Da Fang, was a native of Tiantai. He was a dharma successor of Gulin;

he did not attend to minor details and lived with a carefree and unrestrained ease. He was on good terms with Zhou Yi-qing, the Prefectural Governor. After Da Fang resigned from his duties at the monastery, [he departed].
I was staying at the quarters of the Elder Master Hua at Lingyan. On the eighth day of the ninth month of the Wuxu year of the Zhizheng era, Zhou entered the mountains on business to visit him.
Dafang said, "On the fourteenth day of this month, I shall undergo cremation on this very mountain.
Please wait for me to bear witness. Zhou jokingly agreed and took his leave. On the thirteenth day, [Dafang] sent a verse to Zhou, which began: "Yesterday..."
"Before the cliff I gathered firewood; today this illusory body has turned to dust. I earnestly entrust these words to you, O worthy lord:
when the clouds have cleared from the azure void, there remains but a single sliver of the moon. Zhou received the verse, yet he still did not believe it.

That night, he requested that Hui set up a high platform using dry wood and lent him a small cell to sit in. Hui said, "As for the wood, I shall comply with your request; as for the cell, I have none."
He then pointed to the wooden bench where Huā was sitting and said, "This will suffice. Huā followed his instructions.

On the morning of the fourteenth day, after rising and ascending the hall, he took leave of the assembly of monks and spoke another verse, saying: "My former body was originally that of a monk at Stone Bridge;
Thus I came among humans to receive both love and hate. When love and hate are exhausted, the true body is fully revealed: An iron snake chews cold ice within the flames."
He then tucked dry firewood into his sleeves and ascended the wooden platform. Holding a torch himself, he set the wood ablaze until a fierce, blazing fire erupted.
Amidst the mass of flames, he offered incense and recited: "The numinous sprout does not belong to the seeds of yin and yang; Its root originally comes from beyond the kalpas.
Were it not for Xiuju’s personal revelation, How could it be transplanted here into the midst of fire? He then passed the rosary to Huacheng and said, "This is merely—"
Upon receiving the final testament, Zhou Wen went to the site where the flames had reached and obtained many śarīras. He marveled at this beyond measure.
Having constructed a stūpa for the relics at Lingyan, he further composed a poem in lamentation, which says:
When the Yuan troops descended upon Jiangnan, Xian Mo’an of Jinshan was coerced by Bayan and placed within his tent, accompanying him to Wulin.
At that time, Master Xuewu Ke of Zhongzhu had already resigned from his monastic duties, as the imperial throne of the Song had been transferred elsewhere.
Mo’an, who deeply knew the Master and held his spiritual conduct in high esteem, spoke of him to Bayan and requested that he be appointed to ascend and reside at Lingyin Monastery.
Mouan personally carried the invitation letter to knock at the gate. The Master pulled back the bolt, revealing half his face, and asked, "Who are you?
Mouan replied, "I am your old friend, so-and-so. The Master dropped the bolt and said, "I do not know you.
Although the Master lived beyond the mundane world, he maintained himself with loyalty and integrity; thus, he felt no need for the summons from Lingyin and resolutely rejected it.
It was thus. At that time, there was a head seat among those present who was over eighty years old. He sighed and said, "I was born in the Song dynasty and have grown old in the Song dynasty;
yet I shall not die in the Song. I shall now sever all food and die. He then ceased taking grain and passed away.
Within the monastic community, hearsay is never to be relied upon as evidence. Later generations transmit that Dahui and Fozhi studied together under Yuanwu;
Yuanwu was particularly fond of Fozhi, while Dahui was often dissatisfied with this. Subsequently, Fozhi resided at Yuyang.
Daehye followed in his footsteps, but on the pretext that the sand and water would be unfavorable, he opened the stupa. Yet the true body remained undecayed;

Daehye used a pickaxe to break open the skull, poured oil into it, and set it ablaze. If this is indeed the case, it may be called an act of extreme cruelty—something even ordinary people would find unbearable, yet Daehye endured to do it.
I once read the epitaph for the stupa of Beopji, which states that he performed *jāva* (cremation).

Regarding the enshrinement of *śarīra*, there has never been a case of an entire body being interred within a stupa. Furthermore, while Master Xiaoweng was residing at Yuyang, he was occupied day and night with the restoration of its ruins.
It happened that the seat at Tiantong was vacant; the Imperial Secretariat submitted a memorial, and by imperial decree, the Master was appointed to fill it.

The Master, however, as the construction works at Yuyang were not yet complete, submitted a petition to the Chancellor requesting exemption from the transfer. [He argued that] Tiantong was essentially the same as Yuyang. Yuyang...

The King’s words were indeed those of Tiantong. For the Master’s monastic regulations were strict and solemn; he showed no leniency toward any transgression by his disciples, and all stood in awe of him.

Consequently, seeing that he had declined the invitation from Tiantong, some maliciously conspired to spread slanders, claiming he had purchased the position at Tiantong for one hundred thousand coins.
To this day, the ignorant continue to pass this down as common gossip. I, Yuanzhao, have previously [investigated] this matter.

During the Zhizhen era, [Wang Yinglin] visited Yajingwen at Pufu Jiaosi Temple. Jingwen produced for him the original ink manuscript of the Master’s letter addressed to the Chancellor, through which he first realized that his previous accusations had been unfounded.

Furthermore, upon reading the biography, the epitaph for the Three Pagodas, and other works within the *Wuwen wenji*, it was found that the accounts of the Master’s resignation from Tiantong were identical in intent to the meaning of the letter. Indeed, the Way of these two masters was...

The sun and moon adorn the heavens; there is nothing that does not receive their illumination. Yet, there are those who spread groundless slanders. Although such things are insufficient to defile the Master, they nevertheless must be refuted.

Master Qianshai of Lingyin was a native of the region south of Zhejiang. He was a successor of Yujie. A scholar who composed literary works, his vision regarding the contemporary world was as clear as the empty sky.
He once authored the *Treatise on Supporting the School and Manifesting Orthodoxy*, which analyzes the distinction between heterodoxy and orthodoxy and adjudicates right from wrong with great merit.
However, within it, he takes the master’s brandishing of the mallet and raising of the whisk as the handle for his discourse, citing the example of Prince Wang Yan of the Jin dynasty grasping...

The jade fly-whisk and the fact that its color matched that of his hand serve as proof. Now, when a patriarch strikes the mallet or raises the whisk, he is manifesting the supreme point of the ultimate path;
how could this be a trivial matter? Yet, for Qianlai to treat it as a mere conversational prop not only shows he has lost the true eye of his own house, but also misleads future generations.
After the Yuan dynasty had extinguished the Song, Yang Lianzhenjia was appointed as the General Superintendent of Buddhist Teachings for Jianghuai.
By imperial decree, he ordered the opening of the tombs of the Southern Song emperors at Mount Shanyin in Yue. Zeyun Meng, the abbot of Yanfu Monastery, accompanied Lianzhenjia;
however, it was he alone who insulted the remains of Emperor Lizong, surely out of long-standing resentment. Meng’s intent lay solely in flattery and compliance with Lianzhenjia.
He also kicked him in the ribs with his left foot. Before long, a man in Yangzhou died suddenly and arrived at the realm of King Yama.
A messenger reported: "The Son of Heaven from the world of the living has come. King Yama descended from his throne to welcome him. [The messenger] saw the yellow canopy and the left-hand banner;

chariots and horses were packed together in dense throngs, no different from the ceremonial retinue of a worldly sovereign. Once he was seated, after a short while, a ghost-soldier appeared, leading a monk bound in shackles.
He was led before the palace hall. The Son of Heaven of the world of the living interrogated him, saying: "I have occupied the throne for forty years.
In governing the state and the people, I have certainly committed no great transgressions. Regarding your teachings, I have never failed to promote their circulation.
I bear no grudge against you; why then do you falsely accuse me? You have also excessively insulted me. He then commanded his fierce warriors to pierce his left foot with an iron awl.
[The executioner] raised his thumb high and struck him with it. The sound of his agony was a piercing, wretched cry, unbearable to hear.
After a brief moment, [the executioner] withdrew. A man who had died a sudden death asked in astonishment, "Who is the Son of Heaven in the world of the living?
Someone replied, "It is Emperor Lizong of the Song. He asked again, "Who is the monk being beaten? [The reply was: "It is Zeyun Meng, the abbot of Yanfu Monastery in Hangzhou."
A man who had died suddenly revived. He then went to Yanfu Temple to inquire about the matter in order to verify what he had seen;
however, Yunmeng’s left big toe had developed a sore that could not be cured, and he had already passed away.

Among the preeminent figures of our school in recent times, there have certainly been many who, in their immediate application of the Dharma, did not follow the old tracks of the ancients, yet were able to exercise their own wisdom to open the minds of others, thereby suddenly increasing the weight of the teachings by nine-tenths.

Why is it that such individuals are so rarely seen today? For instance, there was the Dharma Master Yi of Fengshan at Lower Tiantzhu in Hangzhou during the Yuan dynasty’s Yanyou era. [End of fragment]

At the beginning, he was granted the title of *Sanzang* and the rank of *Hongluqing*, yet he did not accept its emoluments. Whenever there were even slight discrepancies within the Buddhist teachings, he would invariably rectify them.
Prince Chen of Goryeo, the son-in-law of the Emperor, received an imperial decree to pay homage to Avalokiteśvara at Mount Putuo.

Upon passing through Hangzhou, he took money from his carriage and established a vegetarian feast at Mingqing Temple for the abbots of all the mountain monasteries, as well as for the provincial officials and those below them from various government offices.

The gatekeeper personally supervised the proceedings and arranged the seating order. The Prince of Shen sat in the center upon the Dharma seat in the lecture hall, while the various officials took their places in order around the seat.

The abbots of the various mountains were lined up along the two corridors. Once everyone was seated, the Master arrived late and proceeded directly to the seat, asking the Prince, "For what purpose is today's vegetarian assembly?
The Prince replied, "It is a vegetarian feast for the abbots of the various mountains. The Master said:

He said, "Great King, you have already stated that you are hosting a vegetarian feast for the various mountains. Yet, as the host, you now occupy the seat of honor while the mountains are lined up along both corridors, some even sitting upon the floor.
How does this differ from the *luo-zhai* (barbarian-style feast)? In terms of ritual propriety, I fear this is not appropriate.

Upon hearing this, the King was filled with shame and remorse, apologized, and immediately descended from the Dharma-seat. He stepped forward to bow to the various mountains, establishing the proper distinction between guest and host.

The officials withdrew to their positions in the two corridors, followed by the abbots of the various mountains. When the meal was finished, the King took the Master’s hand and said, "Were it not for my teacher, our rites might well have failed.
Ah! Is not Fengshan the very person who, through his timely and skillful application of means, is able to open the hearts of others?"
When Master Xugu took his leave of Mount Yangshan to proceed to Mount Jing, he arrived within the city of Yuanzhou.
Offerings of gold, money, silks, and bolts of cloth from donors from all directions were piled high before him. Xugu declined them slowly, saying, "I am not gifted enough.

Yet, the various mountains of the two Zhejiang provinces, because I am somewhat familiar with the essential principles of our school, have appointed me to the seat of Mount Jing, desiring that I open the hall to preach the Dharma and propagate the teachings."

I am merely proclaiming the essential tenets of our school; how could I be held in contempt for my poverty? I request that you return the gifts you have sent, so as to avoid the reproach of being like those who newly embrace the *Avataṃsaka*.
I entrust my attendant monk with only my personal requisites to carry with him.
During the Tianli era, I visited Zen Master Yiyuan Ling at Fengshan on Lake [Hengzhou].
Because I could not resolve the kōan concerning Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the Old Lady of Mount Tai, one day while attending him, I brought it up for the Master’s consideration.
The Master said, "In my youth, I served as the *kanna* (rector) in the assembly of Venerable Fangshan of Ruoyan in Taizhou; I too once raised this very case with that master."
I examined the case. Master Shanshan said, "Venerable Ling, try and offer a turning word. At that time, I spoke offhand:
"All the people in the great earth are helpless against this old woman. Shanshan said, "I am not like that; all the people in the great earth are helpless against Zhaozhou.
At that moment, it was as if I had obtained food when hungry, or as if I had broken out in sweat when ill; I felt a sense of profound joy and liberation. Thus...
He said, "Attendant, try and offer a turning word of your own. At that time, I simply gave a bow of greeting and departed.

I recall that when the Master first entered the monastery, he ascended the hall and cited the public case of the World-Honored One ascending the seat and Mañjuśrī striking the gavel. He commented on it, saying:
The World-Honored One spoke it wrongly; Mañjuśrī transmitted it wrongly; today, Xinfengshan has cited it wrongly. Do you understand?
"After a document has been transcribed three times, the characters 'wu' and 'an' become 'ma'. At that time, the former master Zhu Yuan was living in seclusion at the Six Harmonies Pagoda.
Upon hearing this, he remarked with admiration, "Among all the elder masters nominated by the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs, only Fengshan is somewhat superior."
Master Zi was a native of Ninghai. He was a disciple personally ordained by Yunfeng of Mount Jing and succeeded Fangshan upon his emergence into the world.

As a person, he was compassionate, patient, and forbearing; he never grew weary of exhorting and instructing others. When he passed away, everyone—whether they knew him or not—lamented his loss with deep sorrow.
The Buddhist sutras state that in the ocean there are fish as large as mountains, upon whose backs grow great trees;
day and night they are buffeted by the winds of karma, their suffering beyond comparison. Zhuangzi also said: "In the Northern Sea there is a fish called the Kun; the Kun is so large..."

One cannot know how many thousands of li it was. In the *zhèng* year of the *zuǐmǎo* cycle (1363), someone came from Nurula and said that nearby there were fish as large as mountains passing through the sea, raising their fins and gills and exposing their dorsal ridges and tails above the surface of the water.
Facing north and heading south, it moved steadily away for four days and four nights before its body finally vanished from sight.
This is what is called a "large-bodied sentient being," whose form is thus evoked by the karmic retribution of past deeds.

Yet, when the Asura King stands in the midst of the great ocean, his body equal in height to Mount Sumeru and capable of tossing the sun and moon about with his hands, this fish appears to him as nothing more than a small fry. To the people of the world...
"Everything within the range of one's ears and eyes seems precise and certain; yet everything beyond the reach of the ears and eyes is considered to be mere fabrication.
Alas! This essential compendium of the Chan school was composed by Master Tan of Xue Shan.
When Xue Shan relied upon Chan Master Fang Shan at Ruiyan in Tiantai during the Chunyu era of the Song dynasty, the creation of this collection—how could it have been undertaken lightly?"

When I was young, I once relied upon Master Linggong of Fengshan. During a night assembly, the Master suddenly spoke of the essentials of the school, drawing out points where the ancients had failed—a level to which others could not reach. He then bestowed upon me a volume and commanded that I read it.
More than forty years later, Tianyi Qingyehai re-carved the woodblocks; his resolve is truly commendable. Having [received] this myself...

Preface. Furthermore, I sought out the preface by Master Zhang Jun, in which both state that [the compiler] stole another’s completed collection on Mount Snowy to publish as his own, citing Master En’s single remark regarding the "Severing the River" as proof. Moreover, he divided it into ten fascicles, taking a single phrase from each original chapter as its title;
thus, he has mangled and fragmented the work, losing its essential meaning in many respects. I am concerned that future readers may not discern this.
The reason for this is that [the master] reversed the ocean of karma and disparaged the Snowy Mountains; therefore, I record it.
Dongzhou and Lingyin Dugu were from the same hometown and studied together; their bond of friendship was very profound.

During the days when Dongzhou resided at Tiger Hill, he happened to be serving as the abbot of Wanshou Monastery in the city. The various mountains intended to nominate Dugu to take over the abbacy. At that time, Dugu...
He resided at Tianning Monastery in Huzhou. He ascended through the successive stages; it was not by skipping over them.
Dongzhou tried to dissuade him with all his might, but Dugu took no notice of this. After more than a year, Dongzhou arrived in Huzhou on a pilgrimage and wished to see him.

Carrying a sense of inner shame, he did not go to see him, fearing that Dongzhou might incite others against him and ruin his spiritual endeavors. Therefore, he waited for Dongzhou’s death before going to visit him. Dugu...

I received the report and returned immediately. I treated him with the utmost courtesy, providing him with lodging and grain, and further donated from my private treasury to assist him in his journey.

We spoke at ease regarding our friendship, which was no different than it had been in the past. When he eventually returned from Dongzhou to Huqiu, we met late at night in the Shuangge Hall of the Abbot’s quarters.
As we walked together, I reproached myself, saying: "Dugu is a man of noble character and long life, while I am a petty man. I observed those of the present day...

Among those who are friends within the monastic community (*saṃgha*), they quarrel over the space of a single word or the gain of a single thread, going so far as to slander one another and seek to cast each other down.
They harbor such resentment that they wish nothing more than to sever the other’s life immediately to satisfy their own hearts.
To find someone with the magnanimity of Dugu Ji or the self-reflection of Dongzhou is rare indeed. Generally, when a disciple relates to his teacher, he should conceal the teacher’s faults.
To promote what is good, following the right and turning one's back on the wrong—this is called filial piety.

To conceal what is good and promote what is evil, turning one's back on the right and following the wrong—this is called unfiliality. If a teacher has no good qualities to promote, it is permissible to remain silent.

To force goodness upon them and cause them to be subject to private criticism, only to have their own failings exposed in return, is not something that can be followed; it is permissible to remonstrate against such a person. To force...
To follow such [a path] and cause others to engage in private criticism, only to denounce it as wrong, is likewise unfilial.
I have observed closely that when eminent masters of recent times have passed away, their disciples have prepared formal petitions to request renowned officials to inscribe epitaphs for their stupas.

These invariably record how their parents had extraordinary dreams at the time of their birth, and how, after their death and cremation, their teeth, prayer beads, and other items remained uncorrupted, with *śarīra* relics appearing.

Regarding the enumeration: if these numerical categories were absent, one would not be established as a venerable elder (*bhadanta*). These are all unworthy disciples who, failing to understand the correct principle, have fabricated false claims that bring disgrace upon their masters.
Can this be called filial piety? Among the one thousand seven hundred *kalyāṇamitra*s (spiritual friends) of the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), there are none like this.
Among those who possessed śarīra relics, there were only fourteen individuals. In Venerable Jiyin’s *Biographies of the Sangha Treasures*, there are eighty-one individuals;

among them, those with śarīra relics number only a few. Furthermore, that which our school values lies solely in the "penetration of the essence" (*zongtong*) and the "penetration of the teachings" (*shuotong*).
Those who possess the "claws and fangs" directed upward—those who untie the adhesions and remove the fetters for others—are said to be transmitting the Dharma and delivering sentient beings;

all other matters are merely secondary. As for the fact that, upon cremation, there are occasionally instances where the sense organs remain unimpaired and *śarīras* flow like pearls, this is surely proof of the pure cultivation practiced throughout their lives;
how could such things be easily obtained? I fear that those who come after will successively imitate [such anomalies].
This is effective. He concocts false words to falsely extol his teacher, engraving them upon stone and having followers of heterodox teachings read them;

thus, they instead come to suspect that the ancient sages possessed supernatural powers, which likewise constitutes a fabrication. The harm this inflicts upon the Dharma-gate is certainly no small matter.

How tragic! Dongyang, while residing at the monastery, was falsely accused by a monk from the corridor. He appealed the matter to the Xuanzheng Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs), which issued a mandate appointing Liaohan, the abbot of Benjue Monastery, along with the Prefectural Governor, to adjudicate the case of right and wrong. Liaohan said, "Dongyang has steadfastly adhered to the monastic regulations..."
The rope restrains the multitude with solemnity; those below must not act with license. Therefore, they rashly initiate litigation, desiring only to remove me.
Now that I am among my peers, while the officials sit idly in the hall of the yamen, Dongyang is being prosecuted.
How can I bear this? He immediately retired to the Southern Hall. Chu Shi resided at Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing, where he encountered the local authorities rebuilding the official quarters.

Timber and stone were lacking. It was intended to requisition materials from abandoned monasteries in nearby villages that had no resident monks to meet the requirements. Consequently, the abbots of various temples were assembled to deliberate on the matter.

At that time, Chushi (Chushan Zhenke) forcefully argued that it should not be done, attempting to dissuade them; however, the authorities would not listen. Thereupon, [the opposing party] struck the drum to signal their withdrawal.

They returned to Tianning Monastery in Haiyan. Both elders were courageous in their practice of righteousness; they regarded the abandonment of their esteemed positions as masters no differently than discarding worn-out sandals.
Now, though they are beset by repeated calamities and afflictions, they still remain patient and lingeringly attached—how truly singular is this!

Master Yunwai was a native of Changguo. From birth, his physical stature was slight and small, yet he possessed an abundance of vigor and spirit. In preaching the Dharma, he was able to employ skillful metaphors and indirect allusions;
he desired to humble himself to accommodate his students and guide them to completion. When it came to his soaring eloquence, he transcended all others, leaving no dust behind.

Even those with the eyes of a hawk or the pupils of a dragon would have no way to peer into his depths; the transmission of this singular school of Dongshan relied solely upon him. In his later years, he resided at Tiantong, where eminent monks from all quarters gathered.
The Master was neither arrogant nor conceited; he did not amass wealth, nor did he consume offerings for himself. Whatever alms or benefits he received, he distributed immediately to others.
Upon meeting those of younger generation, he treated them with ever greater reverence, aspiring to uphold the lineage of the School. At both the morning and evening meals, he partook of the gruel.
When it came time for the midday meal, he would invariably carry his alms bowl himself to the hall. After his passing, he left no remaining assets;
thus, fellow practitioners pooled their funds to provide for his funeral expenses. His disciples—Dafang, Shuyudu, Xingyuan, and Zheng Wuyin—were sufficient to expand the school’s influence.
However, their ranks did not match their virtues, and there were none who truly inherited his Dharma, with only one or two individuals remaining under Wuyin’s lineage.

Wen Ruguan was a man of unfathomable character. His style name was Zhiguizi (The One Who Knows His Return). Having studied early at the academies of learning, he subsequently entered the monasteries of Chan.

He followed his nature and delighted in the Way, unconstrained by minor formalities. His mind alone was fixed upon the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī); even in moments of haste or distress, he never for a moment forgot it.
He took pleasure in practicing the calligraphic styles of the Jin dynasty and in painting grapes; both of these arts reached the pinnacle of excellence. Whenever he arrived at various temples...
Upon parting, he invariably demanded money; according to what he received, he would go to a butcher’s or a wine-seller’s shop to buy wine and drink alone.
He would then distribute the remaining coins to the street children, ordering them to lead the way while shouting in unison, "The noble sir is coming! It was for this reason that he was seen.
He would frequently pursue them in groups and compose verses that surpassed those of antiquity. He eventually passed away at Jiao Temple on West Lake.
Some say he was reborn into the family of Bai Zanyuan; perhaps his worldly karmic ties were not yet exhausted, and thus he brought them to an end?
Zhuzhuang Yan resided at Doushuai in Tai. He possessed a natural breadth of character from birth and regarded his seniors with equanimity; consequently, many were jealous of him.
During the previous year’s Qianqing Festival, each prefecture and county was required to select and invite a presiding abbot from among the various mountains to preach the Dharma.
Zhuzhuang happened to be appointed for this duty. Many of his detractors purchased a portrait of Chan Master Rong and used it to pose difficult questions, intending to thwart his eloquence.
The administrative official (zhishi) took notice and reported it in detail. Zhuzhuang said, "The management of doors and general affairs is the responsibility of the administrative official;

ascending the seat to preach the Dharma is the duty of the abbot. Do not speak further. The next day, he went to Tianning Monastery and sat in the guest quarters of the abbot’s hall, conversing and laughing with ease with the masters from various mountains.
When the drum sounded, he rode in a carriage to the Dharma Hall to face the assembly of officials.
After bowing in greeting, he ascended the seat. Once the incense offering was concluded, he adjusted his robes and took his place. Monks came forward to pose questions in rapid succession;
Zhuang responded to them with effortless fluency. Moreover, he was able to turn their own words back upon them for further inquiry, such that some were forced to retreat in defeat.
In this manner, four or five more people [spoke]. The assembly of officials grew weary of standing for so long, so they stopped the rest from coming forward to ask questions.

Thereupon, he took up the essential points and raised the core topics; his discourse was as swift as a whirlwind and as fierce as a clap of thunder, rolling like lightning and racing like shooting stars. Everyone else was exhausted, yet I alone remained with surplus strength.
As for those who harbor jealousy toward him, even if a single person were endowed with ten million tongues, they could not surpass the mouth of the one who offers praise.
It is a pity that his lifespan was not long; it was not due to a lack of merit within the monastic community.
Huangyan Lingshi Xingu-fan first met Dongzhou Yuhui at Tiger Hill (Jiuhua), where he was entrusted with the keys to the treasury. Later, he met Master Zhuyuan at Hongfu Temple.
One night, he went to the abbot’s quarters to seek instruction, saying, “I am contemplating the koan ‘The dog has no Buddha-nature,’ yet I find no point of entry.
I hope the Master will grant me some guidance. The Master replied in a stern voice, “Night! (or: "The night!").
Shenxiu descended. Gufan returned to the hall and scolded him, saying, "If you would not explain it for me, that was the end of it. Why must you show such anger?
Someone reported this to the former master (Nanyue Huairang), who said, "He will understand it himself later. Upon hearing this, Gufan attained sudden, vast enlightenment.
He entered the world [as a teacher], offering a single incense stick as an offering for his former master.

Baoyun Wenzong of the Zhou dynasty was a native of Xiangshan. He was profoundly learned in both the doctrinal teachings and meditative contemplation, and he maintained the Vinaya with great strictness.

Ordinarily, when speaking with others, he was slow and hesitant, rarely venturing a word; yet when ascending the seat to establish the principles of doctrine, his exposition flowed like water pouring from a jar, unstoppable.
At the time of his death, he ascended the seat to lecture on the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*. Having finished the entire scroll, he wished to [address] the assembly...
The disciples stepped forward from both sides and said, "Master, you have not yet entrusted us with your final instructions; how can you pass away into stillness?
Zongzhou replied, "For those of the monastic family, when it is time to go, we simply go. What 'final affairs' are there? The disciples pressed their request even more earnestly.

Thereupon, he descended from his seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters, where he settled every matter one by one. He then joined his palms and recited the names of the Four Holy Ones of the Western Paradise.
Having completed his dedication of merit and the making of vows, he entered nirvana. He was cremated, and the *śarīra* relics were brilliantly radiant.
Master Zhuyuanxian, hearing that Yiruan had purchased many texts from western Zhejiang and brought them back to Taibai, sent a letter to Liaotang in which he wrote:
"I have heard that Yiruan has purchased many texts and brought them back; I imagine there is nothing else [of concern], only..."
"I merely wish to instruct a few fledgling monks. You may tell them: 'Why do you not simply cease? It is like a hound chasing a hare;
it follows its tracks all day long without losing them, yet halfway through the chase, it sees a deer and abandons the hare to pursue the deer, failing to catch either.
What a pitiful state! When I was at Montang on Mount Jing, I once wrote this letter."
He inquired after his late teacher’s well-being, and the teacher replied with a letter, saying:

"Whether you are at the charcoal brazier in the meditation hall fiddling with the fire tongs, or in the midst of speech and laughter, or drinking soup or water—it is all your own self, and nothing other than yourself.
There is no direct practice that transcends this. He further surmised that at that time, the late teacher must have regarded him as...
I am base and unworthy, insufficient to withstand your fierce blows and kicks; therefore, you have graciously shown me this teaching.
This is precisely like picking up yellow leaves to delight a small child, mistaking them for gold. Otherwise, why would you be so mired in such "mud and water"? Alas!
Though the Master entered nirvana more than thirty years ago, these words of instruction feel as if he were facing me in person.
As for Cheng Daoyuan: while remaining in the secular world, he studied under Master Hutang; upon leaving the mundane realm, he attended upon Master Xugong at Mount Jing.
He once composed the *Ten Volumes on the Essential Points of the Study of Nature*, which provided great benefit to worldly instruction. In the丙申 (Bingshen) year of the Zhizheng era...

It was compiled and published by Xi He and Gao Shiming. At that time, Zhang Shicheng occupied Suzhou and arrogantly assumed the title of King, with figures such as Zheng Mingde, Chen Jingchu, and Ni Yuanzhen serving him.
These scholars used the book to refute Huian (Zhu Xi), arguing that his discourse on human nature had missed the essential point.
They presented this argument to Shicheng, who ordered the woodblocks to be destroyed. For human nature is vast and empty.
It is tranquil and solitary; vast and empty, it is beyond all traces. How could it be categorized by good and evil?

To discuss it as being mixed with good and evil and equated with the qualities of *qi* (material force) would certainly be a distinction made against the primordial Dao. I have heard that when Yu heard a virtuous word, he bowed;
when Yan Hui obtained a single instance of goodness, he cherished it and took it to heart. Now, the various Confucian scholars all hold Yu and Yan Hui in the highest esteem.
Yet his conduct differed from that of Yu and Yan. Why was this?
Monk Gulin resided at Bounim; his reputation for the Way was so eminent that those occupying the position of Great Master at the time were envious of him.
Although there were vacant seats among the great masters, few were willing to recommend him. When Tiantong Yun’wo passed away, Yuan Wenqing Gong was serving in the Hanlin Academy;
he specifically sent a letter to Xueya at Wanniu Monastery in Mingzhou, stating: "I once met Elder Gulin at Tiger Hill;
his spiritual edge was steep and sharp, and his discourse was as pure as ice and snow. He is truly capable of supporting and revitalizing the declining winds of our tradition. Now..."
The seat at Tiantong remained vacant, and although even a commoner like myself felt deeply constrained by this, Xueya was the one most worthy to be appointed.
Consequently, I was included among those selected for the position; yet, I failed to succeed. How regrettable!

Chan Master Chang of Xuedou was a disciple of [Master] Hengshan. His appearance was austere and unrefined, and his eyes could not even recognize the character "ding" (the first letter of the alphabet).
He devoted himself solely to the practice of dhyāna-concentration. The gāthās and verses he composed blended principle and phenomenon seamlessly, with rhythms that were harmonious and flowing;

they possessed great power to inspire and enlighten others. Consequently, his contemporaries all referred to him as "Chang-Dharma. I first met him at Mount Jing when I was young, and I still remember him even now.
I remember four verses he composed, titled "The Iron Ox," "The Sea Gate," "Bitter Bamboo Shoots," and "Cessation Hut.
Regarding "The Iron Ox," he said:
Rolled out from the furnace of a hundred refinements, his head and horns are formidable and his body is utterly free of dust.
He cannot be struck, nor can he be pulled; this time, he truly shall not enter the sea of the womb. Hai-men said:
The karmic winds blow up waves like mountains; how many old fishermen find it difficult to set foot upon them?
Only by risking one’s life and casting away the body can one force one’s way in; only then does one know that the jade door was never locked.
Kūsu said: “It is bitter bamboo shoots. He said: [This is so.]
The purple robes are stripped away until one is white as silver;

turning one’s body within the hundred-boiling cauldron, those who have experienced such bitter suffering will not believe it, yet when one happens to bite into it, its flavor is entirely precious. Xichan said:
At the top of the hundred-foot pole, cease asking for the way; on the solitary peak and highest summit, nurture a life of leisure.
Although this broken hut offers no shelter from the blue sky, it is difficult to explain one’s private possessions to others.
Generally speaking, a resident abbot must exercise strict control over his servants and attendants, and should also instruct them constantly with what is good. Only then—
One who does no evil remains free from entanglement. Qian Lai resided at Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing;
his servant stole a dog from a neighbor, boiled it, and ate it, whereby Qian Lai acquired the nickname "Boiled-Dog. Jing Shi resided at Chengtian Monastery in Gusu;
while traveling by boat to attend a donor’s invitation, he passed through a village where his servant stole a sheep from a resident, boiled it, and ate it, whereby Jing Shi acquired [the same].
Regarding the names given for cooking sheep: as for those who steal dogs and those who steal sheep, what concern do they have with one another?

Yet it is they who bear the ill repute; this is surely because ordinary people fail to maintain strict discipline and rigorous instruction. Those who come after should likewise take those two individuals as a warning.
Now, as for the "Abbot" (zhuchi): he dwells in the realm where the wisdom of all bodhisattvas abides, and he protects and sustains the wheel of the True Dharma of all Buddhas.
This is what is meant by the "abiding and sustaining of the Buddha-sons," a title established by Baizhang; how could it have been merely accidental?

In recent times, those who hold the office of Abbot for the sake of fame or profit do not understand the gravity of the responsibility involved. Among them, there are even those who seek only social connections.

Worldly people are preoccupied with eating and drinking. Alas! How lamentable this is! At Hongfu Temple on Mount Shishi in Taizhou, the monk Fanchen was friends with a worldly man named Fang Gongquan.
They took turns preparing meals for one another and spent their days engaged in feasting. There was a monk at the temple named the Superintendent Fang who sought the position of storekeeper;
he had already received a favorable response, but Gongquan, out of private resentment, slandered and obstructed him. Superintendent Fang harbored...
Frustrated and resentful, Fang Jian sent a servant with a gift of tea worth ten feet square. He placed poison within the tea to kill Gongquan.

Gongquan, who deeply revered Shishan, took his own teacup and offered it first to him. Having received the poisoned tea, Shishan died. Fang Jian, believing he had mistakenly poisoned Shishan, was constantly filled with anxiety and suspicion.
One day, hearing the cry of a *sanghu* bird, he associated its sound with the words "Shishan has killed me. His fear and dread intensified further, and so...

A sick man, fearing the light of heaven, bit through his straw mat and died. Tracing the origin of this, it was simply because he did not maintain his proper station, associating with worldly folk and listening to their words;
thus, he ultimately lost his own life. Should those who come after him not take warning from this?
As for the bird *sanghu*, country folk call it the "hammering and grinding" (*duanmo*) bird; it begins to sing at the end of spring, and its sound is conventionally likened to that [of hammering].
It was for the sake of Master Zhang that he forged and polished [the blade]. This monk took it to mean that Master Fang would soon kill him;
it is like "Carrying the Gourd," "The Fried Cakes," "Taking Off the Trousers," and "Muddy Slips"—all of which derive their names from sounds.
As for the Venerable Grand Master, he was Yingguogong, the young ruler of the Song dynasty. After he had submitted to the Great Yuan, Emperor Sacan commanded him to shave his head and become a monk.
The Imperial Preceptor personally rubbed the crown of his head and conferred upon him the secret precepts and dharmas.

He refined them with such precision and firmness that many efficacious responses were already manifest. During the reign of Emperor Yingzong, the Grand Master spontaneously composed a poem, saying: "I send word to Linhe..."
Jing. "How many times has the plum flower bloomed? The guests atop the Golden Terrace shall no longer be able to return home.

The spies reported that the intent of this poem was to incite the people of Jiangnan; they heard of it by the Emperor, who had him arrested and executed. White milk flowed and overflowed, and the Emperor repented.
He ordered the gold from the inner treasury to be ground into paste and issued an edict for a monk skilled in calligraphy to assemble [the remains] at the capital of Yan.

He commissioned the transcription of the honored scriptures of the Great Canon to assist in providing merit for the deceased. In the early summer, the Emperor set out for the capital; while en route to escape the heat, he met his assassination.
Consequently, the newly transcribed scriptures were left unfinished, with less than half the canon completed.

In the year of Xinchou during the Zhizheng era, there was a young boy from a commoner's family in Shaanxi who was only three years old. One day, while in a village lane, he encountered a county magistrate riding through on horseback with his attendants shouting "Clear the way!
The boy charged forward, called out the official’s name, and bowed, saying, "It has been quite some time since we last parted; I hope you are still in good health."
The magistrate was astonished and said, "How could this child know my name? He then approached him and questioned him further.
The child spoke of his name and lineage from a previous life, and furthermore recited several poems he had previously exchanged with the magistrate.
Only then did the magistrate believe that he was indeed an old acquaintance. The child spoke again to the magistrate, saying, "Since parting from you, I have now attained a human body."
"I have passed through three lifetimes. First, after dying, I became a dog. Loathing that state, I bit the child of my master; the master, enraged, killed me.
I was reborn as a quail, and again loathing it, I threw myself into a river and drowned. Now I have attained human form and am meeting you once more—this is a great fortune.
I heard that in his previous life this child delighted in playing with the *I Ching* (Book of Changes) and used its principles extensively before he had even moved."
A single realization. Thus, one enters life and exits death, yet remains unswayed by the transitions of birth and death. Master Māyī named the *Yi* (Book of Changes) the "Mind Changes" (*Xinyi*);
Master Cihu named it the "Self Changes" (*Jiyi*). How profound this intent is!
When Master Po’an retired from Zifu and went to Jingshan, he was invited by Meng’an to appoint him as the Head Seat (Shouzuo) for the ordination of monks.

Among them was a senior monk named Bao, who possessed great insight and understanding. Whenever he encountered the Abbot or the Head Seat opening the hall for formal discourse, he would invariably respond with sudden, sharp wit, seizing the initiative to triumph over them.
One day, when Po’an opened his private room for instruction, Senior Monk Bao arrived. Po’an gave him a critical phrase (chuyu), saying:
"Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a treasure. As soon as it was proposed, it was struck out.

At that moment, the Treasure waited for Pō'ān to finish his statement before speaking. Since it had been struck out while he was in the midst of his discourse, the Treasure thought, "Pō'ān has intentionally disparaged me," and so it slipped away beneath his robe.
After the cremation, the local people collected the relics and presented them to Pō'ān. Pō'ān... [text ends]
Anan picked up [the bowl] and said, "Venerable Baoshang, even if you had eight bushels and four pecks of śarīra relics, set them aside against the wall;
first return to me that one turning of words from before your birth. He threw it to the ground, where only pus and blood were seen. I heard this from my predecessors.
In the *wuchen* year of the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty (1356), Zhang Shicheng captured the city of Suzhou. His younger brother, named Jiuliù, entered the city first and selected a residence.
Upon seeing that Chengtian Temple was secluded and spacious, he took pleasure in it and intended to replace it with a palace.
He ordered his soldiers to destroy the Buddha statues within the palace. The soldiers, fearing both punishment and the consequences of their karma, did not dare obey his command.
Enraged, Liu Jiuliù personally drew his bow and shot an arrow that struck the face of the honored image; he then destroyed everything completely. He welcomed Shi Shicheng to reside there.
On the day of Dingyou, the Great Army of the present dynasty attacked Lükou and Huángdài. Jiuliù supervised his troops in battle, was defeated, and captured. His right arm was severed, yet...
Later, he was executed on the day of Wuxu. Fang Guozhen was appointed as a Vice Commissioner of the Provincial Administration Commission for Jiangzhe and stationed at Mingzhou.
A subordinate official named Liu Renben was quite fond of literature;

he compiled his own past poems and essays into a volume, carved woodblocks to print and circulate them, and used the Buddhist scriptures from the monasteries within the city, peeling off their covers to serve as book wrappers for his work.
The scriptural text was transcribed from poetry. When we behold it, though our hearts ache and our bones suffer, there is nothing that can be done about it.
In the first year of the Hongwu era of the Wu dynasty, the great army captured Mingzhou, and Guo Zhen surrendered. The imperial court then enumerated Renben’s crimes of disloyalty.

He was whipped on his back until it festered and his liver was exposed, and he died. [The numbers] nine and six. One was merely a brave man who did not understand the distinction between sin and merit; such a person might still be forgiven.
But as for Renben, he studied the teachings of Confucius and yet could bear to commit such an act. Confucius said, "Revere the spirits as if they were present.
How much more so should one revere our Buddha, the Great Sage of the Three Realms? Therefore, while one of the two men destroyed the image, the other abolished [the practice].
As for those who committed such writings, before their feet could even turn, they all received the retribution of the ultimate punishment.
Now, as for that which is repaid, it is truly a repayment by oneself; it is not our Sage who repays them.

At the official lecture hall in the city of Yīn, there lived two monks together. One monk was plagued by mice; he constructed a trap using two pieces of wood—one large and one small—to catch them with a mirror-reflection mechanism.
Once the trigger was set and the mouse was caught in the trap, the monk hurriedly went to fetch water, intending to drown it.

His fellow monk, unable to bear it, secretly lifted the wooden boards and released the mouse. The next day, the monk who had set the trap went elsewhere. That evening, the other monk was staying alone.
He saw a swarm of rats making an extraordinary amount of noise. Annoyed, the monk said, "I let you out last night; have you come back to disturb me?
When he rose early the next morning, he found a green cord on his bedside table and was deeply suspicious of it. Several days later, the monk used the cord to bind his waist.
A neighboring monk pointed at it and said, "This is my property; I once lost it in my bedchamber. How did you get it? The monk then related what had happened.
It was only then that he realized the rats had gathered their party that evening to steal the neighboring monk’s sash as a token of gratitude;
this was why they were so noisy. In the *Juefan Sengbao Zhuan*, the original title was *Baichanshi Zhuan*.
When Dahui first saw it and read it, he excised nineteen individuals and burned the work. Later, Juefan sent a letter to the Venerable Zhi of Huangbo, saying:
Zonggao has privately observed that nineteen individuals from the *Biographies of Our Hundred Chan Masters* were subsequently burned;
I do not know his intention. Although Juefan was momentarily displeased, those nineteen people were ultimately not included in the volume.

I have often seen people discuss the *Monk-Treasure Biographies*, noting it stops at eighty-one entries, as if wishing to conform to the number nine times nine. This was merely the proposal of a man from Yan.
This is the account of Iron-Mirror (Tiejing) Wuheshang.
He resided at Heshan. Among his disciples was the monk Gōng, a native of Siming, who maintained himself with integrity and purity and cultivated the Brahma-conduct with diligence.
He recited one volume of the Lotus Sūtra daily. At the time of his death, he experienced no illness or suffering; he simply changed his robes and sat upright.

He passed away. Upon cremation, his tongue remained unburnt. A man from the lakes and seas composed a verse in lamentation, which has been recited by those capable of speaking it down to the present day.
Once, while sitting in meditation at night, he spoke a verse that said: "The single lamp in the mountain window has burned its oil to the dregs;

The hearth stove lacks fire and is cold and still. I shall leave this point of inquiry to be raised tomorrow; The practitioner strikes the bell and ascends the tower once more. He specifically ascended [the hall] for the "Iron Mirror" ceremony.
The Master praised this.

Later, while I was visiting Nantang at Benjue Temple, during a night sitting, we discussed how there is a distinction between "practicing" and "being thorough and decisive" when working on *wugong'an* (critical phrases).
He then cited a verse by the former Master Xiuju for sending off a monk: "Like a silkworm making its cocoon, it binds itself; a hundred turns..."

A thousand layers stand before one’s face; when they are torn asunder, the whole body is fully revealed. The entire family has boarded the ferry at the riverhead. Dongzhou provides a verse in the same rhyme:
"In movement and stillness, how could there ever be entanglement? Why need one further penetrate that which precedes birth? A thousand miles to my old garden—I now return;
on land there is the journey, on water there is the boat. He further says: "The 'Resting in Non-Abiding' (Xiujju) is subtle and precise," yet it seems...
My practice of meditation lacks the exhilarating vigor found in the Eastern Land.
In my youth, while residing at Chokmoknyang on Mount Phŭngsan, I would cast aside my fatigue after meals by playing with friends using a "Selecting the Buddha" diagram.

When Master Yiyuan heard of this, he ordered the head janitor to escort him there. He spoke a verse: "The hundred thousand Buddhas and all sentient beings— Cease striving to measure them within a painting.
