Master Dongyan was a native of Jiangxi. At the age of eighty-one, the fourfold assembly requested him to take up residence at Tiantong.
At that time, Tiantong was in a state of decline following its previous neglect; the Master, mindful of his advanced years, felt he could not rest easy while bearing such a heavy responsibility.

He summoned three of his disciples—Dong, Yuan, and Qing—and assigned them their respective duties, saying: "Dong, I have a karmic affinity with the officials and common people of the Jiangxi region. You..."

"In former times, you proclaimed my will: to acquire wealth for the construction of the Wanshou, Qianyuan, and Baoge pavilions, and to cast bronze for a thousand Tathāgata images along with their ritual implements.
You shall take charge of this. [He said: 'Yuan, you are well-versed in administrative affairs; you shall preside over the local government offices within the city.
[He said: 'Qing, you are cautious, prudent, and sincere; you harmonize those above and below. As the calendar is examined and found to be deficient, it is only you [who can rectify it]. "
He was capable. You were charged with overseeing the construction of the robe-storehouse (*cīvarakuṭī*). In less than five years, the storehouse was completed with all its images and furnishings.

He then used the surplus funds to purchase a plot of land for a sea-dyke field at Mount Xiangshan. As for the ritual vessels for the *dānabhaiṣajya* (alms and medicine), the local authorities remained peaceful and the people, high and low, lived in harmony and solemnity.

Although this was achieved through the efforts of three individuals, had it not been for the Master’s long-standing rules and training, how could such a result have been ultimately attained? Recently, I have seen...
As for those who act as teachers to others, their primary concern lies in swelling the ranks of their own faction.
They regard the neglect and decay of the permanent endowments (changzhu) as a traveler ignores a discarded shed by the roadside, paying it no heed at all. How truly lamentable this is!
Master Duanqiao was stern and unbending in his character; he was extremely cautious in granting his approval to disciples.

During his tenure at Guoqing Temple, Yongxiangtan served as the Head Seat (Shouzuo), Goutiandao as the Secretary (Shuji), and the name of the Librarian (Zangzhu) has been lost. At the commencement of the summer retreat, he presided over the distribution of the whisk (bingfu).
Ascending the hall to express his thanks, he said: "When the Head Seat sees a senior come, he does not concern himself with praise.
The words of the Record Keeper’s discourse are like a painted figure; all the details are complete, yet it merely lacks the final dot in the eye.
As for the words of the Librarian’s discourse, I do not know what he was saying at all. Yet one day in the future, he will surely say, 'I came to serve under the old monk.'"
This is because those who take up the responsibility of the Dharma are unwilling to diminish their own prestige even slightly, leading later students into confusion and error;

though they claim to suppress such behavior, they actually seek to bolster it. Those who preside over the Dharma today lack clarity in their own vision and strive instead to please others with sweet syrup and honeyed water, hoping thereby to win them as dharma-heirs. Alas! If Duankiao were to see this...
This frivolity is not merely a matter of spitting upon and reviling him.
Jia Jixiang of Puzhao Temple in Zhenjiang was a native of Shandong; he was dark and thin, with skin resembling that of a Buddhist monk from India.
In his youth, he sought to leave secular life at the behest of his parents; however, they rebuked him, citing the lack of progeny as a grave failing, and thus compelled him to marry.
He fathered two sons before finally obtaining permission to become a śramaṇa. There, he studied the discipline of *Vijñaptimātratā*.

In the twenty-fifth year of the Yuan era, Emperor Sacan established thirty-six Imperial Lecture Halls throughout Jianghuai, and Puzhao was appointed to one of them. By imperial decree, the Master was charged with presiding over it.

Outside of his lectures, he read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* daily, making ten fascicles his regular practice. He was a close friend with Wunian of Yun'an, who was a preeminent master of the Vijñaptimātratā school.
When the two discussed Buddhist principles in detail, if Wunian occasionally made a slight error, the Master would correct him with precise words;
Wunian never failed to submit with sincere conviction. At the time of his death, he underwent cremation, and the resulting śarīra were exceedingly numerous.
His disciples preserved his remains as bone-relics, enshrining them in a lacquered casket for twenty years. Only then did they construct a stupa at Mount Yushan in Dansi.

When the day arrived for the relics to be placed within the stupa, they opened it to inspect; they saw only śarīra beads adhering to the inner linings of the casket, clustering together like swarms of bees or ants.
When touched, it sparkles brilliantly. Many people among the populace of Zhenjiang have painted its image and enshrined it in temples, calling it the "Auspicious Buddha.
In the autumn of the *guimao* year of the Yuan Zhizheng era, the monk Zian of Haihui Temple in Mingzhou purchased a mountain at Baocang Market.
He built a hermitage on high ground and cleared the site, where he discovered three ancient graves; he filled them with earth. Once the hermitage was completed, he fell ill, and one night—

In a dream, he entered the city of Fengdu. There were three men whose robes and headgear were extremely ancient; they knelt in rows before the Lord of the Underworld and petitioned on behalf of An, saying: "An, in another life you were surnamed Zhao and named Shihong.
You once served as an official and, through private bias, unjustly exiled us to distant places. Including you, there were four of us who suffered this injustice.
Now that we have all received general amnesty, one person has cultivated pure deeds in life and shall be delivered to transcendence upon death. As for us three, however—"
He died earlier and was buried here with me; now he has come again to destroy my burial site, which is indeed a profound grievance. Originally, we intended to execute him together.
However, considering that while he served as an official he once provided for eighty monks, and that he has now been able to become a monk himself, I did not dare do so.
The Lord of the Underworld summoned Dao’an before him and rebuked him, ordering him to restore the land. Dao’an accepted his reprimand. Upon waking, he suddenly heard—
"His words of sincerity shall not fail three times. On the following day, he prepared a pure feast and commanded the withered tree to preach the precepts;
the sick man’s illness was immediately cured. Thereupon, he dismantled the hermitage, restored the horse's mane, and departed.
The Archivist Shi was a native of Dancheng; his name was Quan, and his courtesy name was Hengfu. His father, Xianfu, was a high official at the Southern Surveillance Commission (*Nantai*).
In the *Xinchou* year of the Zhizheng era, he met with me in Ningbo and highly praised the immense merit of Buddhist recitation and chanting.

He further stated that he had personally witnessed two instances which were beyond doubt. In the capital city of Yanjing, there was a scholar who constantly recited the *Tianzhuzhou* (Heavenly Lord Mantra). Suddenly, one—
In the evening, an old man with bushy eyebrows knocked at the door and addressed him, saying, "I am no ordinary man, but a dragon.

Because I failed in my duty during the rains, the Supreme Deity has issued a reprimand against me. I pray for your protection. The scholar replied, "What sagehood do I possess that I could protect you?"
The old man said, "The merit of you reciting the *dhāraṇī* of the Heavenly King is immeasurable. Having spoken these words, the old man vanished.
Several days later, while my left thumb was aching slightly beneath the nail, I looked at it and saw a tiny object like a thread.
It was three or four *cun* long, red in color, and shaped like a dragon. The scholar continued to recite his incantations as before.
That night, the old man arrived again and thanked him, saying, "By relying on your protection, I have escaped harm. I pray that you will now extend your hand out through the window.
When he complied, in a brief moment, thunder and rain broke forth violently; they saw only a dragon parting the heavens as it flew away. There was confirmation of this from Jin’ing.
The scholar was fond of sitting in meditation for over twenty years. One day, he informed his family, "I am going. Thereupon, he sat and passed away.
His family pushed his body down to lie upon a pillow, whereupon he called out, "Do not do this! Do not do this!"
He immediately leaped up and entered the pond, where he died. Thereafter, whenever he encountered relatives or old friends, he would call out their names and converse with them as if he were alive;
sometimes he would ask for wine to drink, and people would drip wine into the pond for him, to which he would reply, "I have finished.
This continued for half a year. Later, there was a monk begging for alms who arrived at his house and heard human voices being made from within the pond. The monk—
He shook his staff and shouted, "Twenty years of sitting in meditation—where is your spiritual work? Because of this, [the master] became silent.
In his later years, Master Shi was extremely diligent in Chan practice and recitation; it was due to these two matters that he gave rise to faith.
In the fifth year of the Hongwu era, I was a guest at the Jiqing Jingshe (Accumulated Blessings Hermitage) on Xiagaih Lake in Shangyu.
One morning, a lady named Yu arrived from Baiguan Market and knelt before me for a long time, declaring: "I and my husband have not been in harmony.
I resolved to cultivate the Pure Land some seven or eight years ago. Recently, during the past year or two, whenever I sit in clarity..."
While sitting in meditation, I heard the sound of subtle music and the cries of cranes and magpies drifting through the air.
I thought to myself that a sublime realm had manifested before me, yet others said it was a demonic vision. I requested the Zen Master to resolve this for me.

He replied, "This is because you have heard in the sutras that when the wind blows through the rows of trees made of a hundred jewels, their sounds are like those of hundreds of thousands of musical ensembles, as well as various birds."
These sounds are texts produced simultaneously by many voices. Once faith in them is firm, they take root within the field of the eight consciousnesses and cannot be removed.

It is only within the state of tranquil concentration that they manifest to the ears. If you encounter this scene again in the future, do not conceive thoughts of it being superior, nor do you conceive thoughts of it being a demon;
you should simply sit down with it and settle it once and for all, and you will see that it is nothing but mind.
"The Pure Land is the primordial nature of Amitābha; it is the entirety of all things. How could it lie beyond the distant lands of a hundred thousand million worlds?
Then, pointing his finger at his own chest, he said, "From this moment on, my mass of doubts has dissolved."

Chan Master Qiujiang Zhan of Guangxiao Temple in Taizhou was a native of Duangjiang in Huangyan. In his youth, he entered the monastic order at Huacheng Temple in his hometown and shaved his head there.
To the right of the temple stood a rock cliff of extreme height and prominence known as Songyan (Pine Rock).

At its summit were the foundations of Falun Temple, originally established during the Tang dynasty of the Five Dynasties by Chan Master Qin; however, as it had long been abandoned, the site was overgrown and its traces obscured. One day, the Master...

When he arrived at that place, he gazed upon it at length and was unconsciously moved by a sense of melancholy. Like a long-traveling guest suddenly returning home, he felt such deep affection that he could not bear to leave.

Thereupon, he sat in meditative concentration beneath a massive rock nearby. When the local villagers heard of this, they encouraged one another to bring him food and contributed funds to hire craftsmen for construction.
Within a few years, a monastic complex had been established. Furthermore, he built a stupa on the ridge behind the temple to serve as a repository for his remains.

He calculated that one day, he would oversee his disciples as they went to the pagoda. He then dispatched messengers to send out invitations everywhere to all those who traveled to and fro, arranging for them to gather at the mountain on a specific date to perform a separate funeral rite.
When the appointed time arrived, monks and laypeople gathered in great numbers. The Master then ordered Fahuan, Zhuchi, Xindao, Yuan, and others to prepare a meal for the living sacrifice.
The assembly was struck with wonder and astonishment, thinking that the Master had grown old and frail; yet the Master urged them on even more.

In haste, he hurriedly prepared the ritual implements and performed the sacrifice. The Master sat upon the hall and received the food; the remainder was distributed so that every member of the assembly partook of its flavor.
The patrons and others read the liturgical texts and wept; the Master also shed tears. Thereupon, he rose and entered the cave (*yǎn*), where he sat in meditative repose.
At that time, the donor Zhou Hengzhi requested a eulogy for an Avalokiteśvara image, and the assembly also begged for a final verse of farewell; the Master granted them both with great swiftness.
He took up his brush to write. A short while later, he passed away; it was the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the [blank] year.

The Master’s final instruction was that his body should be buried and the grave sealed while the flesh was still warm. The assembly could not bear this, so they did not close the tomb until the following day, erecting a stupa over it.
Regarding the Master’s clan name and his lineage of dharma succession and public ministry, these are found in the biography composed by Zhuyong Zhang Jun.
Master Xin of Daochang and An was a native of Wuzhou. He was a successor of Xueyan of Yangshan and possessed genuine practice.
Monastic practitioners from all quarters who were earnestly seeking to investigate and clarify the matter of birth and death delighted in following him.

Several bhikṣuṇīs also requested to lodge their bedding in front of the hall to listen to the Dharma along with the assembly. A group of unruly individuals, whose requests for positions and employment had been denied, falsely accused the Master of being intimate with the bhikṣuṇīs.
Sishang and Luàn were pursued to Hangzhou and detained at the Wumò residence for one night. There, they passed away without illness. Upon cremation, their *śarīra* (relics) were brilliant and pure.
Those who had slandered them were punished for their crimes. Píngshān of Línghyìn succeeded to their Dharma lineage.
Master Xueyan of Yangshan was a native of Wuzhou. His resolve was exceptionally lofty; he would not associate with those who were not his equals.
In his youth, he met Wuzu at Mount Jing while the latter was supervising the casting of a bell and ordered him to compose a preface for it. The Master composed a verse, which said:
"The entire body is but a single mouth, Rolled forth from within the hundred-fold smelting furnace. After sending the setting sun back to its rest," [he adds: "it speaks again."

He urged Mingyue to ascend the tower and pavilion, and subsequently appointed him to serve in the Attendant’s Office (*shisi*). When his term of office was complete, Quanzhun requested someone else to take over his post.
The Master did not wish to have anything to do with this man; as soon as he saw Quanzhun entering the gate, he leaned over the window railing and made a very violent sound of vomiting.
Quanzhun understood his intention and remarked, "This fellow has no merit. Only after the appointment had been canceled did the Master receive [the position].
Regarding the illness of vomiting blood, [his teacher] was greatly incensed. The Master (Wuzu Fayan) paid it no mind at all.

When he entered the world [as a teacher], although he frequently brought up the "fragrance of the Dharma" (the *xiangzong*) in his sermons, it did not take root in others. It is said: "Upon the broken蒲團 (pútán, meditation mat), the earth cracks and heaven collapses;

this is not obtained from others," and so forth. Furthermore, [Wuzu] carried incense and took his seat [to seek instruction]; when he reached Yangshan, it was only then that Wuzhun (Nianchang) burned it away for him. Yet, there still remains [the teaching of] Wuzhun.
These are indeed unfounded and baseless words. I say that Xueyan, being young, was driven by an arrogant temperament, while Wuzu was a patriarch of an entire generation;
unable to exercise forbearance, they caused such a rift in their father-son relationship. All those who occupy great monasteries and hold the fly-whisk should take this as a mirror for themselves.

Master Zhongfeng was a native of Hangzhou. Having entered the monastic order under a teacher to receive the full precepts, he resolved to investigate the Way with single-minded determination, vowing not to rest until he had reached the inner sanctum of the ancient masters.
At that time, Master Gaofeng—who held the "contract" of Yangshan and Xueyan—resided at Simian Rock on Mount Tianmu.
He established a "death barrier," swearing not to admit any monks. Upon seeing the Master, he was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him a *huatou* (critical phrase) for investigation.

The Master applied himself with diligent vigor and sought resolution through inquiry. While reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, upon reaching the passage concerning "shouldering the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgata," he attained a sudden and profound awakening. From that time forth, his wisdom and eloquence became unimpeded.

From sovereigns and high ministers above, down to the eminent scholars of the Three Teachings below, there were none who did not submit with sincere devotion to inquire after the Way. His writings and recorded sayings, such as... [text continues]

In total, there were ten scrolls. His disciple T’ien-chu collected them all and submitted them to the imperial court for inclusion in the Tripitaka. The Master was subsequently posthumously honored with the title National Teacher Puying.
The Master’s physical frame was robust and imposing; whenever he slightly lowered his head, he would gasp for breath. He always sat with his eyes fixed straight ahead.
Whenever requests were made for Dharma words, two *dhūtas* would carry the paper, and he would write upon it with a free hand as it flowed from his brush.

Chan Master Bunan was a native of Dinghai in Mingzhou. Having received the essential instructions from Gao Feng, he once composed verses in succession to Yongming’s *Shanju shi* (Poems on Mountain Dwelling).
His poetic intent was no inferior to that of his predecessor, while his phrasing was more mature; in some respects, it even surpassed the original.
At the time of his death, he composed a verse and passed away while seated in the Guizidang Hall in Central India. After the cremation, many *śarīra* relics were found.
Chengzhiyan resided at Tiger Run in Hangzhou; initially, he studied under Bunuo, and subsequently, upon meeting Tianchi Yuanweng Xingpu, he attained realization and inherited his Dharma lineage.
The assets of Tiger Run had always been meager, yet there were several dozen monks there whom the Master supported daily.
He provided for them with his alms bowl, never flagging even during the bitter cold or the humid heat. When he grew old, he manifested illness and passed away while sitting in meditation.
Later, Shigu Yu saw Jie’an at Daochang Monastery. He subsequently lived in seclusion on Mount Xiapu in Wuxing, maintaining himself through austerity and refusing offerings from donors.
If he happened to run out of food, he would drink only water. By nature, he was compassionate and gentle, taking pity on all living beings. He composed...
This was a verse spoken to rouse and inspire him; he was truly a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for the final age.

Chan Master Wujian was the son of the Ye family of Xianju. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations, yet he possessed such brilliant talent that he served as the internal secretary for Tianning and Gutian.
He visited Chan Master Fangshan at Ruiyan, where he fully grasped the essential points of the teaching. Suddenly, he took Kaizang with him...
The Master went together with them to Mount Huading. Seeking out the old site where Song Ga’ān had resided, he built a thatched hut and settled there.
Thereupon, his spiritual influence spread widely and students gathered like clouds. Laypeople and monastics alike believed that without fields one could not support a large community;

they frequently brought land deeds to offer as gifts, but the Master rejected them all. Throughout both winter and summer he wore but a single robe, and his food was sufficient only to stave off hunger; he made no distinctions.
Regarding the coarse and the subtle: during his cremation after passing away, clear water suddenly gushed upward from the center of his chest like the pouring of water from a jar.
He obtained śarīra relics as large as beans, which dazzled the eyes of those who beheld them; they remain to this day, enshrined and venerated within the mountain.
The head seat Duanya Yishou went to study under Gao Feng. Because their conversation did not reach accord, [Gao Feng] pushed him off, and he fell all the way to the very bottom of a precipice.

That evening there was heavy snow, and the assembly suspected he had already died. The next day, when the snow cleared, his fellow practitioners brought firewood and torches to search for him at that spot, intending to cremate his remains;
however, they found the Master sitting upright beneath an ancient tree on a flat rock. They shook him—
He then opened his eyes and looked around in all four directions, unaware that he had been pushed down into the snow and cold. Upon returning, he went again to visit Feng;
Feng silently marveled at him. From this time on, his reputation for the Way grew daily, and both monastics and laypeople took refuge in him.

Whenever anyone asked a question, he would strike them only with his staff, never revealing a word or a breath of air, requiring them to realize it for themselves. In recent times, most masters have relied primarily on verbal explanations to guide others, whereas—
Only our Master was not so; he was truly worthy of admiration.
The Venerable Benyuan of Mount Jing, whose name was Shanda, was a native of the Zi clan in Xianju.

In his youth, he traveled as a mendicant with Master Xigan Xin, vowing never to hold formal administrative office. He resided at Jiangxi and met Xueyan, following the assembly into the master’s room for instruction. One day, Xueyan—
Observing that his character was outstanding and his deportment measured and disciplined, [the Master] wished to appoint him to the position of Hall Superintendent.
The Master consulted with Ji’an, who said, "I and you once made a vow; can it be broken now? The Master consequently desisted. Later, he returned to Xianju.

The villagers requested that he become their presiding master for the Multitude of Blessings Temple (Duōfú), but he declined and departed. He traveled through Hunan and became the presiding master of Fuyan Monastery.
Fuyan had been a Daoist observatory during the Tang dynasty, which was converted into a monastery by the Great Master Cidi (Dashi). Many of the Daoists were displeased with Chan practice;
the Master vowed that his followers would eventually all serve as abbots there. Among them was one man surnamed Mu and named Daxian, whose name now perfectly matches that of the current Master.
It was merely a matter of confusion. People thus came to know that the Master was a wood-cutter immortal reborn in this world.
Later, he returned to Western Zhejiang and visited Jingshan Xuefeng; upon entering the inner quarters, he attained realization. As the seat at Huiyun was vacant, the Master succeeded him there.
It was there that he first offered an incense stick for Yunfeng. Subsequently, he resided at Baoning, Jingci, and Jingshan, each of which had achievements worthy of record. The Master...
In all his residences, he did not provide sleeping couches; at night, he would hold a candle and burn incense while seated, and at dawn, he would join the assembly—this was his constant practice.
Furthermore, his physical constitution differed from that of others: in severe cold, he wore fine linen and silk gauze, and in heat, he wore silk and cotton wool.
With his surplus funds, he established Dayuan Monastery on the eastern road halfway up Mount Jing to receive visiting monks from all quarters.

Suddenly, one day, knowing that his time had come, he gathered the assembly and finished recounting the events of his lifelong travels as a wandering monk (*yātrā*). After a brief moment, he passed into stillness.

Within the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), some disparaged him because he had not held formal office. However, before Baizhang established titled positions, people were concerned solely with the Way (*dharma*);
those who attained enlightenment regarding the mind-ground and who took up the great Dharma with vigor were, in effect, the leaders of the day.
Resplendent as the heavens, with swift thunder shaking the earth, there is no stream of sentient beings that does not receive his illumination and awakening.
One does not know what offices he held at that time, but would such a person not be worthy of veneration?

Yi was the head seat (shouzuo). His courtesy name was Wuxiang. He was the son of Xia, a military family from the Song dynasty. His physical strength surpassed that of others, and he was most proficient in martial arts.
He had once inherited his father’s noble rank, but finding no pleasure in it, he resigned from office. He enrolled at Fengguo Temple in Shangyu to leave the household life and shave his head.

His master assigned him to recite the Heart Sūtra; however, after three days, Yi could not remember a single word. Because of this, he came to loathe the practice intensely. Suddenly, there was a monk named Shan Miaofeng.
As he was passing by the temple, he said to his teacher, "This man does not know how to read or write, yet he only enjoys sitting in a formal posture;
I fear he has come from a state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). May I have him? His teacher joyfully consented and ordered him to go with him. They first arrived at Xuedou.
Qiufu Guata diligently engaged in investigation, never letting his side rest upon his mat. One day, he entered meditative absorption and remained as motionless as a withered tree.
A fellow monk in the adjacent quarters, the Head Seat Zheng, constantly waited for him. After seven days had passed, Guata slowly emerged from samādhi, appearing joyful and relieved.
Walking leisurely through the corridors during the clear night, Zheng said, "I am glad that the Great Matter has been resolved. Guata did not answer.

Pointing to the bell tower he had seen, he spoke a verse extemporaneously, and so forth. Furthermore, speaking with earnest words, at dawn he struck his mendicant’s staff and traveled with double speed;
in barely two days, he reached Huading Peak. He went to pay his respects to Master Xixi, but encountering the onset of darkness, the gate was already closed.
He consequently stayed overnight outside the gate. At daybreak, the gate opened; he entered and saw Master Xixi, and through their mutual inquiry and examination, he realized the essential meaning.
He kicked over the incense stand and departed immediately. Xixi called him back, but he did not respond and continued down the mountain.

He then went to Tianmu in Hangzhou to visit Gao Feng, with whom his spiritual resonance and discourse were especially harmonious; Gao Feng appointed him as the head seat (*śayanāsana*). At the beginning of the Zhizheng era, he came to Haihui in Mingzhou.
There he dwelt alone in a single room, severing all external ties. His shadow never left the door, and his ritual implements never strayed from his side. All people...

Reverently recorded on the first month of the Jia-wu year of the Zhizheng era. Suddenly, he said to his attendant monk, "I shall go to play for a while in Jiangdong on the twenty-fourth day of next month.
When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, changed his robes, and requested a pair of traveling leggings to bind his feet.

He ordered the monk to support him before the Buddha statue, where he performed three prostrations. Withdrawing, he sat cross-legged and addressed the assembly, saying, "Did I not tell you this the other day?"
On this day, he passed away with an air of serene composure. He was ninety-nine years old. His remains were kept in the shrine for seven days;

his countenance remained bright and clear, and his hands and feet were as supple and warm as if he were alive. During the cremation, only sparks of fire were seen scattering like a multitude of jumping tiles, with no smoke or mist at all.
Once the fire was extinguished, śarīras (relics) were obtained in incalculable numbers.
Miscellaneous Records of Mount Ānanda, Volume Upper;
Miscellaneous Records of Mount Ānanda, Volume Lower.
Narrated by the Tiantai śramaṇa Śākya *Wúyùn*.

Sengjing of Miaojue Qitang in Huzhou was a son of a farming family from Wujiang. Having lost his education at a young age, he received the tonsure and went to visit Miaofeng Xuan, the son of Zhongfeng.
Xuan instructed him to investigate: "Before one's parents were born, who is this that is my original face?
Sengjing investigated in this manner for thirty years without attaining any realization. Later, in Mingzhou...
The monk Zhao of Huayan Temple went to Lake [Chibi] and stayed there with his companions. He was encouraged to recite the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration" from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
One day, while reciting the passage, "When birth and death have ceased, the state of tranquil extinction manifests," he suddenly attained a profound realization.
His entire body was filled with joy, yet he could not speak; he could only dance with his hands and feet. Someone asked him about it.
"Are you delirious? He replied, "The state of quiescent extinction is manifest before me.
On the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month in the early years of the Hongwu era, he said to Master Zhao, "The first day of the eleventh month is my birthday; on this day, I shall pass away.
When the time arrived, he bathed, changed his robes, and offered three pieces of incense: one to Śākyamuni Buddha, one to Amitāyus Buddha, and one... [text ends]
I pay homage to Master Liaogong, the Mountain Lord. He was indeed his preceptor for ordination. Furthermore, he instructed those around him, saying, "Three days after my death, perform the cremation;

seven days later, smelt the bones. I only fear they will not withstand the smelting. Everyone doubted these words, yet when the bones were placed in the furnace, the bone melted and overflowed as liquid.
When the fire cooled, it solidified into a single branch of *lingzhi* fungus, its radiance brilliant and shimmering.
It was brilliant, with five colors intermingled; when struck, it produced sound. Although carved, engraved, painted, or drawn, nothing could surpass it.
To this day, the numinous fungus remains in the Miaojue Period Hall.
The Great Being Haeyun of Gyeongsu Temple in Yanjing was named Injeom. He was a native of Shanxi and surnamed Song.

At the age of seven, his father taught him the "Opening the Sect and Clarifying the Meaning" chapter of the *Classic of Filial Piety*. The Master asked: "What is the 'sect' that is opened? What is the 'meaning' that is clarified?"

His father marveled at this and took him to see Master Yan, who was transmitting the precepts. Desiring to examine his spiritual capacity (*indriya*), Master Yan had him read the "Song of the Thatched Hut" by Master Shitou.
When he reached the line, "Whether it be destroyed or not destroyed, the Lord remains," Master Yan asked, "Where is the Lord?
The Master replied, "What Lord? Yan said, "The one who is apart from being destroyed or not destroyed. The Master said, "This is precisely..."
"This is a guest," [Yan] said. The Master asked, "And what of the host? Yan smiled coldly and remained silent.

He then went to pay his respects to Master Zhongguan Zhao, taking him as his teacher, whereupon he shaved his head and received full ordination. One night, he happened to hear a voice in the air calling out the Master’s name, saying:

"Yinjian, your great task is about to be accomplished. Go; do not linger here. Thereupon, he took up his staff and traveled to Yan. Passing through Songpu, he encountered rain and stayed overnight there.

I frequently had the opportunity to receive instruction from the Elder Monk Kongshi in the Mengyang Hall, listening to his teachings and exhortations, which greatly benefited my spiritual cultivation. Indeed, that elder had personally studied under and seen former masters of high standing.
Xu was endowed with correct knowledge and vision; his learning was comprehensive and vast, and his expositions were lofty and subtle.

Furthermore, he was skilled at instructing students, tirelessly teaching them without weariness. As for his application of the "upward" tongs and hammer [of Zen pedagogy], there was no one who could approach him.
Later, he occupied two famous monasteries in Zhejiang, and eventually retired to live in seclusion on Mount Dabaishan.
At that time, I was in Siming, where I invariably traveled to prostrate myself at his feet during the seasonal festivals.
Three years after my arrival at Mount Zhong, the former resident of Mount Cui, Master Xuanjiding, arrived. It had already been four years since the Elder passed away from Siming. One day—
He presented a volume titled *Miscellaneous Records of the Mountain Hermitage*. Upon reading it, I found that all contained the instructions and teachings I had previously heard from the Elder.
Alas! I longed to see the Elder once more, yet he could not be found again; instead, I have obtained the opportunity to read the treatises he composed throughout his life.
How deeply moving this is! The Elder has another collection of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) circulating in the world.

Some have remarked that while those records frequently offer "pointing directly upward" (*xiangshang nianditi*), this compilation cites the words and deeds of past sages to broaden the learning and experience of practitioners.
Viewing the *yulu* (recorded sayings) as steep and perilous, this [text] is simply plain and easy. Nevertheless, from the outset, there were never two different intentions.
Indeed, the Buddha-Bhagavān had what is called "teaching by adapting to the capacities of beings.

Yet, when the patriarchs raised their staffs, held up their fly-whisks, or raised an eyebrow and blinked an eye, they all sought to provide students with a point of entry; it cannot be said that this compilation is not such.
To act as a guide for others in the upward path—this is indeed possible. A student must first possess the true eye before they can succeed.
Written on the occasion of the Gengwu year of the Hongwu era by Qingjun, the mountain dweller of Linggu Temple.

This *Miscellaneous Records of the Mountain Hermitage* is truly an excellent chronicle of the monastic community; it serves as a remedy to prick the ailments of heterodox Chan and to treat its chronic, terminal illnesses.

I believe this will be of benefit to the present day in Fusang. Nevertheless, as I have not yet seen ancient woodblock editions, errors resulting from threefold transcription have become quite numerous.

Novice students have frequently been distressed by these while reading it. During the intervals of my convalescence, I consulted one or two classic texts and, adding my own critical judgment, managed to establish a rough collation. Wherever there remained any lingering doubts, I have recorded them here.

This is situated beside [the aforementioned]. It is what is meant by "transmitting that which is doubted as being doubted. Furthermore, I fear that two or three individuals have erroneously added Japanese-style punctuation (*wajiten*).

Now, having commissioned artisans to carve the woodblocks, I am deeply apprehensive that there may be no small number of errors. I look up to the literary talents of the Zen community and beseech you not to withhold your compassionate favor, but to trouble yourself once more with corrections.
Written on a day in the second month of spring in the twentieth year of Kōei (1643), the *Kimi* year, at Daimeizan in Tanyō.
Mountain Inscription By the Hermitage-Dwelling Bhikṣu Wenshou (Wen-shou)
